card.title: Fix the last commit
card.blurb: Correct the commit you just made instead of piling an `oops` on top. Fix a bad message, fold in a file you left out, and keep the history the same length.
hero.title: Fix the last commit
intro.0: You hit Enter and spot the typo a second later. The instinct is to stack another commit on top - `fix typo`, then `oops`, then `fix the fix` - and now whoever reads the history has to work out which one is the real change. Git can replace the last commit instead. Here you correct a message, and fold in a file that should have gone in with it.
task.1.title: Fix the typo you can still reach
task.1.context:
Two of these commits have a misspelled message. `git commit --amend` replaces the commit you are standing on with a corrected one and moves `main` onto it, so it reaches exactly one of the two.

Run `git log --oneline` before you type anything. It lists the newest commit at the top, and that is the only one amend can touch.
task.1.goal.0: Read `git log --oneline` - two of these messages are misspelled.
task.1.goal.1: Amend the one on top so the animal is spelled properly.
task.1.goal.2: Leave the other typo alone; the history stays two commits long.
task.2.title: Fold in the file that belongs
task.2.context:
The last commit saved the feeder on its own. Amend rebuilds the commit from whatever is staged right now, so a file you stage first joins the commit you already made.

More than one file never made it in, and only one of them belongs with the feeder. Run `git status` to see what is waiting.
task.2.goal.0: Run `git status` to see what did not make it into the last commit.
task.2.goal.1: Stage only the file that belongs with the feeder.
task.2.goal.2: Read `git diff --staged` - it prints exactly what the amend will fold in.
task.2.goal.3: Amend the commit with the message `set up the feeder`, and leave the other file untracked.
task.3.title: Fix the last commit - recap
task.3.context: One command, and the last commit is a different commit.
task.3.summaryIntro: Amending does not edit a commit. It makes a corrected one and moves your branch onto it, leaving the old one behind with nothing pointing at it. That is fine while the commit is still only yours.
task.3.summaryItems.0.title: Amending -
task.3.summaryItems.0.text: replacing the commit you just made with a corrected one, so the mistake never becomes part of the history.
task.3.summaryItems.1.title: `git commit --amend -m "..."` -
task.3.summaryItems.1.text: gives the last commit a new message and keeps its parent, so the history does not grow.
task.3.summaryItems.2.title: What is staged goes in -
task.3.summaryItems.2.text: the replacement is rebuilt from the staging area, so a file you `git add` now joins the commit you already made.
task.3.summaryItems.3.title: The last one only -
task.3.summaryItems.3.text: amend reaches the commit `HEAD` is on, and no further back.
task.3.summaryClose: Next: naming a commit without its hash, so you can point further back than the last one.
concept.gt-amend.def: Replacing the commit you just made with a corrected one, rather than leaving the mistake in the history.
